opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the key insight is that science isn't just something that happens in laboratories with expensive equipment. It's something everybody does, all the time. A toddler dropping a spoon off a high chair over and over is running an experiment. When you're trying to figure out why your Wi-Fi keeps cutting out, you form a hypothesis, maybe it's the microwave, and then you test it. When you're cooking and a recipe doesn't work, you change one variable and try again. That's the scientific method in miniature.

So when we think about building systems that learn through interaction rather than just passively absorbing data, everyday science is the natural place to start. It captures the core loop we care about: you have a model of how the world works, you notice it's incomplete or wrong, you decide what to do to find out more, you act, you observe, and you update. That loop is what's largely missing from current machine learning. Most of our systems are trained on enormous static datasets. They're very good at interpolating within what they've seen, but they don't really go out and ask questions of the world.

Everyday science is also a good focus because it's tractable. If we started with frontier physics or drug discovery, the experiments are slow and expensive, and it's hard to tell whether a system is reasoning well or just got lucky. With everyday problems, like figuring out the rules of a simple environment, working out how a mechanism works, or diagnosing why something broke, we can run many experiments quickly, we know the ground truth, and we can compare what the system does to what people do. That gives us a much tighter feedback loop for research.

There's a deeper reason too. I don't think "real science" and "everyday science" are separate capacities. The same cognitive machinery, building causal models, imagining counterfactuals, choosing informative actions, being surprised and revising your beliefs, underlies both. Professional science is that machinery scaled up and augmented with instruments, mathematics, and institutions. If we can build systems that do the everyday version robustly and flexibly, we've captured something fundamental, and scaling it to harder domains becomes a question of extension rather than reinvention.

Finally, it keeps us honest about what intelligence is. A system that can answer exam questions about science but can't figure out how a novel gadget works by poking at it hasn't really understood anything. Grounding the work in everyday inquiry forces us to build systems that actually engage with the world, rather than ones that just reproduce descriptions of it.

r001.rationale: It says the same cognitive machinery underlies everyday science and professional science, including causal modeling, informative actions, and belief revision.

r002.rationale: It describes learning about a novel gadget by interacting with it and contrasts interaction with passive training data, but does not present this as an alternative to large-scale imitation learning.

r003.rationale: It does not state whether a system can learn scientifically without discovering new useful science.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the honest answer is that "science" with a capital S, the kind that happens in a lab with a particle accelerator, is actually the rarer and stranger version of something all of us do constantly. When you walk into a hotel room and the shower has one of those unlabeled knobs, you don't read a manual. You turn it a bit, you feel the water, you form a little theory, you revise it. That's an experiment. You're intervening on the world, observing the result, and updating a model. And you do it dozens of times a day without ever calling it science.

That's the thing we care about at Basis with MARA. If you look at how most machine learning systems are built, they learn from a fixed pile of data that someone else collected. They never get to ask a question. They never get to poke the world and see what happens. And I think a huge amount of what makes human intelligence work is precisely that we're not passive. We decide what to look at, we decide what to try, and we're pretty good at choosing experiments that are informative given what we already believe.

So everyday science is a useful target for a few reasons. One is that it's grounded. You can't fake your way through figuring out how a new coffee machine works with plausible-sounding text. Either you get coffee or you don't. The world gives you feedback that's hard to argue with. Two, it's compositional in a way that's really demanding. The hotel shower, the coffee machine, the unfamiliar door lock, they're all different, but you're bringing a shared toolkit of causal reasoning and hypothesis formation to each. We want systems that have that toolkit, not a separate memorized solution for each gadget. And three, it's actually tractable to study. You can build environments where the system has to discover how something works through interaction, and you can measure whether it's asking good questions, whether it's being efficient, whether it recovers when its first guess is wrong.

There's also a deeper point. A lot of the field talks about reasoning as if it's something you do in your head, in isolation. But I think real reasoning is a loop with the world. You have a partial model, you act, the world pushes back, and that pushback is what lets you escape your own mistakes. An agent that only reasons internally can be very confidently wrong forever. An agent that runs little experiments has a way out. So for us, everyday science isn't a toy version of the real goal. It's a pretty direct instance of the real goal, which is building things that can be genuinely uncertain, go find out, and change their minds.

r001.rationale: It describes everyday device troubleshooting and lab science as the same cycle of intervening, observing results, and updating a model.

r002.rationale: It contrasts interactive exploration with learning from a fixed data pile, but does not identify large-scale imitation learning as the approach MARA would replace.

r003.rationale: It presents interactive experimentation as a goal for AI, but does not state that this can be achieved without discovering useful new science.

astra-6.text:
I think everyday science captures something quite fundamental about how we learn. You don’t just sit there receiving observations; you do things to find out how the world works. If something in your kitchen stops working, you form some hypotheses, try something, see what happens, and revise your understanding. It’s a little scientific investigation, even though you probably wouldn’t call it that.

That’s a useful focus for MARA because it brings together learning, reasoning, and action. The system has to work out not only what it believes, but what interaction would help it resolve an uncertainty. And the result of that interaction has to change its understanding in a way that helps with the next problem.

Everyday settings also make that challenge concrete. You have incomplete information, you can’t try everything, and you often don’t know in advance which details matter. So the question becomes: can we build systems that make progress under those conditions, by asking questions and experimenting, in the way people routinely do?

r001.rationale: The response describes everyday troubleshooting as a small investigation, but does not connect it to professional scientific inquiry or state that both rely on the same principles.

r002.rationale: It describes exploratory action and experimentation, but does not present learning to use unfamiliar devices as an alternative to large-scale imitation learning for MARA.

r003.rationale: It says systems can learn scientifically through questions and experiments, but does not state that this need not produce new useful science.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think everyday science captures something important about how people learn. If you’re trying to work out why your plant is dying, you don’t just sit there collecting observations. You water it, move it closer to the window, and see what happens. You have some hypotheses, and you act on the world to distinguish between them.

That’s the kind of learning through interaction we’re interested in with MARA. The learner has to decide what question to ask, what intervention might be informative, and how to revise its understanding when the outcome is surprising.

And everyday settings are useful because you don’t get a neatly specified problem with all the relevant variables already identified. Figuring out what matters is part of the task. So it gives us a way to study learning as an ongoing process of investigation, where understanding helps you act, and acting helps you understand.

r001.rationale: The response describes everyday investigation and learning through action, but does not connect learning unfamiliar devices with professional scientific inquiry or say they share the same principles.

r002.rationale: It describes exploratory action as part of MARA’s learning, but does not present it as an alternative to large-scale imitation learning or mention unfamiliar devices.

r003.rationale: The response frames learning as investigation, but does not state that an AI can use a scientific approach without discovering useful new science.
